Please stop doing THIS in Japan! 7 sushi rules you must know 🍣
Knowing these basic cultural rules makes the experience so much better—and keeps you from accidentally insulting the chef!

Here are the 7 rules:
1. NEVER pass food chopstick to chopstick. 🥢
Why is this such a strict rule? In Japan, this specific action resembles a traditional Buddhist funeral ritual. After a cremation, family members use chopsticks to pass the bones of the deceased to one another before placing them in an urn. Doing this exact same motion with your food at a restaurant is considered extremely bad luck. Always place the food directly on a plate to share!

2. Don't stab your sushi.
Just like rule 1, sticking your chopsticks directly into your food is a major taboo. It looks exactly like the incense sticks offered to the dead at funerals.

3. Don't rub your chopsticks together.
Doing this implies you think the restaurant gave you cheap, low-quality chopsticks that might give you splinters. It insults the restaurant's quality!

4. Never dip the rice in soy sauce.
Only dip the fish. If you dip the rice, it will absorb too much soy sauce, fall apart, and disrespect the chef's hard work.

5. Don't bite it in half.
Sushi is designed by the chef for one perfect bite.

6. Keep your elbows off the table.
In Japanese dining etiquette, bad posture shows disrespect to the food and the people who prepared it.

7. The beautiful mindset of "Mottainai".
Try not to leave any food. You will hear the word "Mottainai" a lot in Japan. It translates to "what a waste," but the meaning goes much deeper. It is about having profound respect for the ingredients' lives, nature, the farmers, and the chefs. Finishing your meal completely is the highest form of respect and gratitude you can show.

Which of these rules surprised you the most?

transcript.text: Think about how differently we travel today compared to 10 years ago.
Your boarding pass is on your phone.
Your credit cards are on Apple Pay or Google Pay, wherever it's supported.
You call an Uber from your phone.
You navigate with Google Maps on your phone.
You manage hotel bookings through an app.
And some hotels even let your phone become your room key.
But there's one problem.
Almost everything we do while traveling now depends on our phone having connectivity.
And you could always buy a local SIM after you land.
But that means finding one, waiting at the airport, activating it or switching SIMs.
Or you could get a travel eSIM, which is convenient.
But you still need to choose a provider, buy the right plan, set it up on your phone.
Or if you're already on V, you can simply claim the international roaming benefit that's already included in your plan through the V app.
That's right.
You can now get free international roaming on multiple postpaid and prepaid packs on V.
And this way you can continue using your Indian number abroad, which I personally love because my banking OTPs and important messages continue to come on my same number.
So just like your flights, hotels, cars, itinerary go with you with your phone, just make sure your connectivity travels with you too for free with V's international roaming plans.

A simple, delicious frittata that makes the most of seasonal courgettes, peas from the freezer and one of my favourite gut-health hacks: cooked and cooled potatoes. Ingredients: 
8 British Lion eggs

2 garlic cloves chopped

1 cup of frozen peas 
1 large courgette grated 
30g each of dilll, parsley and basil 
Rind of one lemon 
125g (1/2 a block) halloumi cheese grated 
1 tsp baking powder 

Optional base:
450-500g of potatoes cooked and then smashed into the base.

Turn your oven on to 180C
1- cover your dish with parchment paper. Take your cooked potatoes and smash them and line the Botton of your baking dish with them. 
2- Mix 8 lions eggs in a bowl with a good pinch of salt and pepper. Set aside. 
3- Add the extra virgin olive oil to a pan and let it heat up gently. Add the zest of one lemon to this and 2 crushed cloves of garlic.

5- Put in the oven and let cook for approx 40 minutes. This will vary slightly according to your own oven.
6- Slice when cooled and enjoy! So Good!

transcript.text: Skip the big chains.
Here are my favourite spots for an enjoyable coffee break in the centre of London.
If you're spending the day in central London, you're probably going to need a coffee break.
Now you'll find any of the big coffee chains on just about every street corner, but why
settle for ordinary?
Here are my top five cool and quirky spots that'll elevate your caffeine pit stop into
one of the highlights of your day.
Just a stone's throw from Big Ben and the Houses of Parliament, you'll find Suzette
Garden, a gorgeous green courtyard that feels miles away from the hustle and bustle of Westminster.
It's a really cosy intimate space with great coffee and a proper local welcoming feel.
They serve coffee and pastries from 7.30 in the morning, or if you're stopping by a bit
later, why not treat yourself to a glass of wine or a cocktail?
Tucked away just behind Leicester Square, the Picturehouse Cinema hives an incredibly spacious
and comfortable first floor bar that serves coffee, drinks and food daily from noon.
Beyond being a lovely quiet spot to recharge, you're sipping coffee inside London history.
The cinema sits within a building that was originally the Trocadero Palace of Varieties,
a Victorian music hall that dates from 1882 and once hosted stars such as Mary Lloyd.
Nestled within a stunning courtyard in the heart of bustling Covent Garden, 26 Grains is a cosy
spot that takes its coffee seriously.
It's popular for its ever-changing breakfast menu, so popping in during the afternoon usually
means fewer crowds.
It's not the cheapest option on this list, but the top-tier brew and gorgeous setting
make it worth every penny.
Just a short stroll from the British Museum, Momo Garden Cafe is a quaint little coffee shop
built inside a wooden hut within a beautiful public square.
Open daily for coffee, homemade cakes and light snacks, it's a total oasis.
If the sun's out, sitting in the garden with a fresh brew is easily one of the most peaceful
ways to escape the hustle and bustle of the city.
Plus, Momo is big on sustainability, their cups are 100% biodegradable and you'll get
40p off your drink if you bring in your own region.
usable one. And finally, for me, the absolute best coffee spot in all of London sits just a
stone's throw from St Paul's Cathedral. Host Café is a non-profit coffee shop built inside the
stunning church of St Mary Aldermarie, a 350-year-old Gothic gem rebuilt by Sir Christopher Wren
after the Great Fire of London. Beyond serving fantastic coffee in a breathtaking setting,
it's run as an ethical, sustainable business by an inclusive church whose primary goal is to give
back to the community it serves. That's it for now. If you want to join me on a free walking tour,
click the link in my bio. And don't forget to follow me for more.
